title: nanomem v3 vs sqlite-vec / Chroma / FAISS -- standardised head-to-head

protocol.evidence_recall_at_k: 1.0 only if EVERY gold paragraph for the question is inside the top-k
protocol.per_doc_recall_at_k: fraction of the question's gold paragraphs inside the top-k, averaged over questions
protocol.recall_at_4_is_a_prefix_of_the_top_10: every arm is queried once at k=10 and recall@4 is the first four of that ranked list. For the exact arms this is identical to querying k=4. For the HNSW arms it is a small ADVANTAGE, because they search a k=10 beam and are then scored at 4.
protocol.embeddings: nomic-embed-text, pre-computed and cached; L2-normalised ONCE by --prep and loaded from the same .npy by every arm
protocol.insertion_order: numpy default_rng(0).permutation(N), identical for every arm, materialised before the ingest clock starts
protocol.reopen: every arm is built, closed, and reopened from disk before it is timed; latency is warm (>=20 warm-up queries first)
protocol.latency: single query, no batching; >= 200 timed queries per arm per corpus (query set repeated when the corpus ships fewer unique questions)
protocol.threads: no arm is thread-pinned; each engine keeps its own default thread policy (this is the 'strongest reasonable config' rule)
protocol.payload: nanomem, sqlite-vec and Chroma all store the document TEXT alongside the vector. FAISS IndexFlatIP stores vectors only, so its on-disk figure is not comparable.
protocol.isolation: one subprocess per (arm, corpus) so ru_maxrss is clean

val1190.gold_rule: all supporting-fact paragraphs, located by the first 80 chars of the fact text (same rule as headtohead_v3.py)

n10000.gold_rule: G[:, :2] gold paragraph indices shipped in hotpot_train_8k_embeds.npz; questions kept in file order, restricted to those whose gold indices are < n_docs, first 500

n71433.gold_rule: G[:, :2] gold paragraph indices shipped in hotpot_train_8k_embeds.npz; questions kept in file order, restricted to those whose gold indices are < n_docs, first 500

engine_stats.active_heap_ram_method: sum of the numpy buffers this vault has ALLOCATED (capacity, not just the used slice) + record bytes + a 64 B/row index estimate; never a constant. It is what the VAULT holds, not what the PROCESS costs: the interpreter, numpy itself and transient copies are not in it. MEASURED GAP, in a process that does nothing but open a vault it did not write and read stats once: 1.10x at 71,433 docs (288.9 MB of RSS growth against 262.0 MB reported) and 1.38x at 10,000 (50.7 MB against 36.8 MB) -- evidence/stats_rss_gap_v3r5.json. Both sides of that gap moved when Arena.reserve became the default: the older figure (1.52x, 612.3 MB against 401.6 MB, evidence/rss_v3r4.json) was measured on an arena that grew by doubling. Use 'process_rss_kb' for the process figure. A CACHED OPEN (`arena_source == 'cache'`) holds almost none of this in the heap at all: the vectors, the columns, the record sections and the id table are clean, evictable, file-backed pages of `<vault>.arena`, counted in 'mapped_bytes' instead. That is why this key can read ~0 on a 71,433-document vault -- the bytes did not vanish, they moved to a page the OS may drop.

config.metric: cosine over pre-L2-normalised float32 (Chroma is given the same normalised vectors as every other arm)
config.note: Chroma 1.5.9's PersistentClient is the Rust core (chromadb.api.rust.RustBindingsAPI) and CreateCollectionConfiguration exposes exactly two index types, 'hnsw' and 'spann' -- both approximate. There is no 'flat'/'exact' option. The Python BruteForceIndex still in the tree (chromadb/segment/impl/vector/brute_force_index.py) belongs to the deprecated SegmentAPI, which a stock 1.5.9 install cannot even instantiate (ModuleNotFoundError: hnswlib). This arm is the closest reachable approximation: batch_size and sync_threshold are pushed past the corpus size so records stay in the unsynced write buffer. See exactness_cross_check for whether that actually bought exactness.
